# **CHAPTER I**  **INTRODUCTION** {#chapter-i-introduction}

English grammar instruction This chapter establishes the foundational framework for SynTutor, an explainable AI (XAI) learning system designed for Natural Language Processing (NLP) driven syntax analysis. It presents the background of the study, detailing the background of the study, core challenges that language learners face when using English Grammar tools. Furthermore, the chapter also outlines the study's statement of the problem, significance and defines key terms to provide clear context for the overall research.

## **1.1 PROJECT CONTEXT** {#1.1-project-context}

	Emerging technologies in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and their integration in language education has made a transformative impact in computer assisted language learning (CALL) into more advanced systems that can adapt to the needs of learners and explain complex theories more easily. Natural Language Processing (NLP) technologies have significantly advanced the capabilities of these applications, opening up new possibilities for machines to understand human language and its complexities (Ansari, 2025). Tools that identify grammatical errors, suggest lexical alternatives, and improve the structure of a paragraph have been widely used in different fields. However, although these models have achieved high accuracy in detecting surface-level syntactic errors and improving sentence structure, they largely operate in a “black box” where explanations are hidden from the user (Deng et al., 2025). Modern tools highlight a given text and provide another sequence, becoming correctors rather than teachers because they do not explain the underlying grammatical reasoning. There is a transparency ceiling as the lack of clarification  leaves learners guessing how proficient sentences are written, creating a dependency on programs that create their work instead of actually improving their independent linguistic competence.  
	To move beyond this “black box” limitation, tools must shift their focus from correcting sentences to a system that can analyze, provide feedback, and generate explanations that enable users to become more proficient. A clear and concise tool that can be utilized by AI to bridge this gap are syntax trees. Syntax trees are used to analyze a sentence’s grammar by providing a hierarchical data structure. It shows a sentence’s grammatical organization which helps learners to identify the relationships between words and phrases. By splitting a sentence into its different constituent elements such as noun phrases (NP), verb phrases (VP), and prepositional phrases (PP), the syntax tree can mathematically illustrate syntactic and dependency relations. The visualization of these rules can enhance learning of learners. Recent studies on English as a Foreign Language also demonstrate how using visual tools can allow learners to understand linguistics and grammatical relationships better than text-based instructions. (Bochari & Hastini, 2025).

	Despite the educational benefits of syntax trees, however, interpreting them manually is too technical and are often challenging for new learners to use alone. This is where Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) becomes an intervention. XAI covers methods to make machine learning systems more interpretable by explaining their decisions to users. With this application, users can not only view the visual structures of sentences, but also receive an explanation they can learn from. The XAI transforms the system into a learning agent, with interpretable, rule-based reasoning that ensures learners do not encounter a “black box”, as they can understand what can be improved on their sentences (Selvi, 2024). The creation of an explainable and accessible phrase-structure constituent syntax tree generator becomes an effective system to help both learners to analyze sentences and become more competent in linguistics. The researchers propose SynTutor, an integrated system that utilizes NLP constituency parsing combined with a contextual reasoning to support efficient identification of grammatical structures. By using XAI, SynTutor automates and explains syntax trees while being an accessible learning application. It is designed to provide learners with structural transparency that grammar tools lack, assisting them in gaining a more profound understanding of linguistics and improving their formal writing abilities.

## **1.2 PURPOSE AND DESCRIPTION** {#1.2-purpose-and-description}

The primary purpose of this study is to develop SynTutor, an integrated educational system that bridges abstract linguistic theory with modern computational methods. By combining AI-driven Natural Language Processing (NLP) with interactive phrase-structure syntax trees, the project transforms traditional grammar instruction into a visual and highly accessible format. The overarching goal is to provide a unified framework that supports both active learner comprehension and advanced linguistic analysis, effectively moving users beyond a passive reliance on surface-level automated corrections toward genuine grammatical competence.

The system creates instant grammar trees and clear explanations, helping teachers deliver engaging, data-driven lessons.

Functionally, SynTutor is designed as an intelligent tutoring agent that facilitates the structural analysis of English text. The system provides a flexible environment capable of accommodating extensive textual inputs, maintaining rigorous syntactic precision by isolating data at the sentential level for processing. Users navigate through their submitted text by selecting specific sentences, which the system then parses to generate a corresponding hierarchical syntax tree. Each tree annotates components with their specific grammatical roles, such as parts of speech, tense, agreement, and modification. Crucially, SynTutor integrates Explainable AI (XAI) to supplement these visual diagrams with clear, natural-language explanations. Rather than simply highlighting errors, the system explicitly details the underlying rules governing each syntactic relationship. This dual approach of sentence-level visualization and rule-based XAI feedback enables users to deeply understand grammatical structures and provides educators and researchers with a practical, real-time tool for demonstrating linguistic concepts.

## **1.3 STATEMENT OF THE PROBLEM** {#1.3-statement-of-the-problem}

Existing Grammar Error Correction (GEC) tools are limited in their ability to elucidate the underlying structural rules that govern correct grammatical construction and are only capable of detecting surface-level errors. As these tools correct without explanation, it leads to learners relying on tools instead of cultivating actual grammatical competence. Although syntax trees are a well-established representation for grammatical structure, existing parsers produce static, non-interactive diagrams devoid of contextual justification or instructional scaffolding, leaving learners with a visual representation of the proper and improper structure of grammar without giving them a deep understanding of the reason.

	Therefore, this study aims to develop SynTutor, an explainable, interactive intelligent tutoring system that supports not only grammatical correction but also explicit grammar learning through structured, visual feedback. Specifically, the study seeks to address the following questions:

1. How can an NLP-based parsing capable of generating phrase-structure syntax trees for English texts, single sentence to extended passages, be implemented?  
2. How can each node of the syntax tree be annotated with its grammatical role and provide natural-language explanations using an Explainable AI component?  
3. How can an interface be designed to be interactive that allows learners to visualize sentence structures, experiment with valid sentence variants, and access explanations for each node?  
4. How can the system provide educators, researchers, and scholars with a tool for demonstrating grammatical concepts, interpreting parser outputs, and diagnosing recurring errors in learner corpora?  
5. Is SynTutor an effective learning tool for improving grammar comprehension, reducing learners’ dependence on grammar error correction tools, and providing understandable explanations?

## **1.4 RESEARCH OBJECTIVES** {#1.4-research-objectives}

### **1.4.1 General Objective** {#1.4.1-general-objective}

	To develop an integrated and explainable AI-based (XAI) system that uses phrase-structure syntax trees to support grammar learning, enable real-time sentence analysis, and facilitate both educational and linguistic research.

### **1.4.2 Specific Objectives** {#1.4.2-specific-objectives}

1. To implement NLP-based parsing capable of generating phrase-structure syntax trees from input text, from single sentences to extended passages.  
2. To annotate each node of the syntax tree with its grammatical role and provide natural-language explanations using an Explainable AI component, making the parser’s reasoning understandable to learners.  
3. To design an interactive interface that allows learners to visualize sentence structures, experiment with valid sentence variants, and access explanations for each node.  
4. To provide educators, researchers, and scholars with a tool for demonstrating grammatical concepts, interpreting parser outputs, and diagnosing recurring errors in learner corpora.  
5. To evaluate the system’s effectiveness in improving grammar comprehension, learner independence, and the clarity of the explanations by conducting a system test and questionnaire to BCS learners and English/Linguist instructors.

## **1.5 HYPOTHESIS** {#1.5-hypothesis}

	The study hypothesizes that integrating NLP parsing with an XAI educational layer can effectively diagnose, visualize, and explain structural grammar in real-time. The hypothesis is as follows:  
**Null Hypothesis (H01):** The integrated neural consistency parser can generate phrase-structure syntax trees with no statistically significant degree of accuracy across varying levels of English complexity.

**Alternative Hypothesis(Ha1):** The integrated neural consistency parser generates phrase structure  syntax trees with a high degree of accuracy across varying English sentence complexity.  
**Null Hypothesis (H02):** Grounding the Explainable AI (XAI) diagnostic engine on the Linguistic Constraint Matrix does not significantly reduce grammatically unsound feedback, resulting in generative hallucinations or unrated edge errors.

**Alternative Hypothesis (Ha2):** Grounding the XAI on the structured grammatical output reduces grammatically unsound feedback, resulting in linguistically verifiable and context-aware explanations.

**Null Hypothesis (H03)**: There is no statistically significant difference in student scores measuring deep-structure grammatical competence before and after using SynTutor

**Alternative Hypothesis (Ha3):** The visualization of syntax trees, combined with the XAI feedback improves a learner’s comprehension of deep-structure grammatical rules compared to traditional grammar-checking software.

**Null Hypothesis (H04):** SynTutor does not meet acceptable usability standards for student learners and linguistic educators as measured by the System Usability Scale.

**Alternative Hypothesis (Ha4):** SynTutor is highly accessible, usable, and reliable, according to the System Usability Scale, as an education tool for both learners and linguistic educators.

## **1.6 SIGNIFICANCE OF THE STUDY** {#1.6-significance-of-the-study}

The development of SynTutor presents a significant contribution to the fields of language education, computational linguistics, and artificial intelligence by integrating Natural Language Processing (NLP) with Explainable AI (XAI) to generate interactive phrase-structure syntax trees. This study provides distinct, practical benefits to the following specific groups:

**For English Learners:** SynTutor acts as a powerful, interactive visual scaffold that transforms passive grammar correction into an active learning experience. Instead of merely accepting generic automated edits, learners are provided with an interactive syntax tree that visually maps exactly how individual words group into phrases and clauses. This visualization serves as an "advance organizer," allowing learners to comprehend the fundamental hierarchical mechanics of language. Furthermore, unlike traditional "black-box" grammar checkers that flag errors without context, SynTutor provides understandable, rule-based reasoning for every syntactical relationship. This contextual feedback empowers students to internalize grammatical rules rather than guess at them, providing immediate, guided practice that reduces their long-term reliance on automated editing tools and ultimately develops them into highly independent and competent writers.

**For English Educators and Teachers:** The system serves as a novel and highly practical instructional resource that can be integrated directly into classroom environments to demonstrate complex grammatical concepts in real time. Teaching deep-structure grammar is often challenging due to its abstract nature, but SynTutor provides educators with the visual tools necessary to systematically prove to students exactly why a particular sentence structure succeeds or fails. By generating immediate, mathematically sound syntax trees paired with pedagogical XAI explanations, the system bridges the persistent gap between theoretical linguistic instruction and practical, engaging application, allowing teachers to deliver more dynamic and data-driven language lessons.

**For Linguists and Language Researchers:** SynTutor offers a sophisticated framework that concretely operationalizes abstract linguistic theory—specifically probabilistic phrase-structure rules—by linking it with real-time NLP capabilities. For researchers, the tool eliminates the tedious process of manual diagramming, allowing them to easily explore sentence variants and test complex grammatical hypotheses instantaneously. Additionally, the system provides a structured methodology for corpus analysis and diagnostics; researchers can utilize the deterministic XAI output to efficiently identify, categorize, and diagnose recurring structural errors within large datasets of learner corpora, thereby advancing empirical research in language acquisition and syntactic priming.

**For the Field of Educational Technology and AI Developers:** From a technical and developmental perspective, this study demonstrates a highly effective integration of NLP parsing and Explainable AI within an educational setting. While contemporary Large Language Models (LLMs) and neural text generation systems achieve high accuracy, they typically operate opaquely, leaving users blind to the underlying logic of their outputs. SynTutor directly addresses the industry's call for transparent and accountable technology by anchoring its AI within a deterministic framework. By explicitly annotating each tree node with its syntactic role and explaining the AI's reasoning in natural language derived from a verifiable constraint matrix, this study provides a working blueprint for solving the "black box" problem in modern educational software.

## **1.7 SCOPE AND LIMITATION** {#1.7-scope-and-limitation}

	This study focuses on the development and evaluation of SynTutor, a system based on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) intended to help with grammar learning by generating and analyzing phrase-structure syntax trees. The system utilizes Natural Language Processing (NLP) to handle English text, in the form of sentences. It provides grammar feedback based on syntactic structures, such as parts of speech, tense, agreement, and modifiers. It also includes an explainable AI feature that gives clear, easy-to-understand explanations for the flagged node in the syntax tree. Additionally, there is an interactive interface that lets users visualize and explore sentence structures in real time. The system is assessed for its ability to improve grammar understanding, usability, learner independence, and the clarity of explanations among Computer Science students, English  students, and English professors from De La Salle University \- Dasmariñas.  
	However, the study has several limitations. The system is limited to the English language and does not support multilingual input. It utilizes constituency-based phrase \-structure trees as its primary structural representation and does not expose dependency-based analyses to the learner; dependency metadata produced by the POS tagger is used only internally for preprocessing and is not surfaced in the interface. The analysis focuses on syntax and does not address semantic meaning, pragmatic context, or writing style. Additionally, the evaluation takes place with a small group of participants from students and professors at De La Salle University \- Dasmariñas. Their technical background may not fully represent the wider target user population. The evaluation also occurs within the timeframe of the thesis, so it does not consider long-term assessment of learner independence, grammar retention, or sustained learning outcomes. This limitation may impact the generalizability of the findings. Finally, the study does not include a control group; therefore, causal claims about SynTutor’s superiority over traditional grammar-checking software cannot be made from the present design.

# **CHAPTER II**  **REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE** {#chapter-ii-review-of-related-literature}

The Review of Related Literature section examines both foreign and local studies concerning the application of Artificial Intelligence, Natural Language Processing (NLP), and Explainable AI (XAI) in the context of English syntax and grammar analysis. Furthermore, this chapter explores the pedagogical effectiveness of syntax trees in language education alongside existing grammatical learning systems to identify the specific gap that SynTutor aims to address.

## **2.1 FOREIGN LITERATURE** {#2.1-foreign-literature}

Extensive literature in computational linguistics highlights the significant potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to enhance linguistic competence. By providing personalized learning experiences, interactive environments, and instantaneous feedback, AI empowers users to refine their language skills with greater efficiency (Rugaiyah, 2023). Given that the future of computer-assisted learning is deeply rooted in these foundations, Natural Language Processing (NLP) and machine learning algorithms are already being extensively applied within the field.

However, for these systems to effectively teach grammar, they must be capable of visualizing and explaining abstract rules to the learner. In linguistics, the syntax tree serves as an effective tool for meeting this need by visualizing the hierarchical structure of a sentence and the relationships between its constituent elements. Understanding these diagrams is crucial for determining phrase structure rules and developing a learner’s analytical abilities. Consequently, integrating syntax trees into computational programs—such as a generator that effectively constructs these diagrams—is highly beneficial for both students and linguists (Karjo & Ying, 2024). SynTutor utilizes this approach to provide a critical platform for advancing a learner's linguistic awareness and structural comprehension.

	In a study conducted by Triana et al. (2025), it was determined that AI can substantially assist in the field of syntactic analysis. The researchers sought to validate AI’s accuracy using specific sentence patterns, emphasizing its role as a supportive tool rather than a primary authority in syntax education. Their findings revealed that while AI demonstrates a high accuracy rate of 90% in identifying subjects and predicates, it maintains a moderate accuracy of 80% for objects and a lower accuracy of 75% for complements and adverbials. Consequently, AI proves valuable for identifying syntactic patterns, and its integration can offer learners a more comprehensive linguistic understanding. SynTutor adopts a similar framework by utilizing syntax trees to explain sentence structures and improve user comprehension.  
A significant advancement in Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the shift from opaque "black-box" models toward interpretable frameworks, as demonstrated by Li et al. (2023) in their study on explicit syntactic guidance for neural text generation. The researchers proposed a top-down generation schema guided by a constituency parse tree, proving that breaking down sentence construction into hierarchical constituent expansions allows for a more "human-like" and controllable process. Crucially for the development of SynTutor, this syntax-driven approach establishes "interpretable pathways" where errors can be traced back to specific structural depths.  
	Ribeiro-Flucht et al. (2024) provide the pedagogical validation for using Explainable AI (XAI) to bridge the "transparency gap" in language instruction. Their research emphasizes that traditional learning models often lack the conceptual clarity necessary for learners to understand why a specific classification or correction was made. The study demonstrates that by employing linguistic complexity measures—specifically phrasal and clausal elaboration—XAI can successfully transform complex data into conceptually understandable explanations. Furthermore, the empirical evidence suggests that XAI methods, such as SHAP, can effectively describe linguistic proficiency for users, thereby encouraging human trust and comprehension. This further validates SynTutor’s core objective of using XAI as a transparent educational tool that maps directly to a student’s developmental needs.  
	Addressing the critical need for transparency in Large Language Models (LLMs), Li et al. (2025) explored the integration of multiple XAI techniques to enhance model interpretability. Their research indicates that as LLMs become increasingly complex, their black-box nature poses significant risks for accountability, which can be mitigated through a combination of methods such as attention visualization, feature attribution, and probing tasks. The study concludes that no single XAI method provides a comprehensive explanation; rather, a combination of different interpretability tools—visualizing what the model "attends" to while probing its internal linguistic knowledge—creates a more robust understanding of the model’s behavior. This research provides the essential framework for SynTutor in developing a transparent feedback system that reveals the "why" behind syntactic rules. By utilizing this diversified XAI strategy, SynTutor transforms the AI from an opaque black box into a transparent digital tutor providing clear, evidence-based guidance.   
Muralidaran (2022) developed a linguistically motivated approach to grammar induction that mirrors human psycholinguistic properties such as incrementality and expectation. The research identifies grammatical structures by recognizing general cognitive patterns of conceptual  organization, moving away from purely statistical black-box models to prioritize how humans naturally assemble and connect linguistic schemas. This shift toward transparency is central to SynTutor’s framework, which rejects black-box corrections in favor of an Explainable AI (XAI) approach. SynTutor aligns with Mulindaran’s emphasis on human-like conceptual organization, grounding its feedback in the hierarchical organization of syntax trees so that the AI’s reasoning is not just statistically probable but linguistically logical to the learner.  
A survey by Bryant et al. (2023) illustrates how Grammatical Error Correction (GEC) has evolved over time, transitioning from rule-based methods and statistical classifiers to the neural machine translation systems that represent current technological advancements. The paper shows significant progress in identifying and correcting common grammatical mistakes, such as subject-verb agreement and preposition errors, as well as semantic inaccuracies. While current GEC systems achieve high accuracy, they are primarily evaluated on technical precision and recall, with little attention paid to the educational value of the feedback they provide. The authors conclude that while technical performance has greatly improved, these tools often fail as teaching resources because they correct errors without providing explanations. This supports SynTutor’s primary assertion that correcting grammar without instructional context prevents learners from developing meaningful grammatical skills.  
According to a study conducted by Bochari and Hastini (2025), it was found that Syntax Tree Diagrams were very beneficial in teaching English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners to recognize structural ambiguities and resolve them through teaching methods using this tool. The researchers used a pre-experimental one-group pretest/posttest methodology involving thirty-five (35) fifth-semester students from Tadulako University, Indonesia. The results indicated that after learning to parse sentences through tree diagrams, there was a significant improvement in the learners' ability to identify and resolve structural ambiguity, and that using visual representations of syntax in the form of syntax trees is more effective than traditional text-based instruction for improving grammatical understanding. However, the study is limited to classroom-based implementation and does not explore how these visual strategies can be integrated into automated or AI-based systems that provide real-time analysis and feedback, which provides strong support for the use of syntax tree visualization in the SynTutor learning environment.  
Through a socio-technical analysis, Farrow (2023) discusses how explainable AI (XAI) can enhance pedagogical practices by demonstrating that the concept of "explicability" is influenced by many external factors and cannot be viewed as having a singular technical definition. The author identifies three essential components of effective explainability: algorithm transparency, appropriate levels of abstraction in explanations, and sufficient detail. The study also distinguishes between interpretability (human readability) and fidelity (the accuracy of the algorithm's internal operation). Farrow explains that for learners and teachers to effectively interact with AI-based educational systems, explanations must match the user's level of understanding rather than relying on expert-level descriptions. However, since the discussion remains largely theoretical and does not present concrete applications for grammar learning, it reinforces the need for SynTutor to provide clear and learner-friendly explanations within its grammar analysis framework.  
Wei (2023) examined the impact of AI-supported language learning on EFL students across multiple areas, including grammar development, vocabulary, reading comprehension, writing ability, and self-regulated learning. In this mixed-methods study involving 60 university participants, the author reported significantly greater improvement for all language learning outcomes among students receiving AI-supported instruction. These results were particularly pronounced in respect to students’ performance on grammar-related tasks. Wei explains that these improvements stem from the ability of AI systems to provide immediate, organized, and personalized feedback that increases learner engagement. However, the study does not explore how AI systems can incorporate deeper structural analysis—such as syntax tree visualization and explainable feedback—to further enhance a learner's understanding of sentence construction, which supports the development of SynTutor as a more advanced learning tool.

## **2.2 LOCAL LITERATURE** {#2.2-local-literature}

The development of SynTutor is grounded in local literature that explores both the technical feasibility of automated syntax tree generators and the practical application of AI-driven linguistic tools within the context of the Philippines. Crucially, such a system requires a high-quality parsed corpus for training, Sagum et al. (2023) addressed this infrastructural need by developing an Automated Filipino Language Treebank Generator. Their study focused on automating treebank generation in the Filipino language, where every sentence in a text corpus is parsed and tagged with its syntactic structure. By classifying and tagging words into specific lexical classes, the researchers established an infrastructure for deeper language understanding. This work directly supports SynTutor’s technical objectives by demonstrating how word-tag pairs can transition to structural visualizations using automated treebank generation.  
Beyond technical feasibility, local research also highlights the need for creating passive and active structural learning for students, a gap emphasized by Cantilero (2025). The researcher investigated the relationship between syntactic priming—the unconscious learning where students reuse recently encountered structures—speech acts, and the overall linguistic competence of Senior High School students in Aklan. Cantilero’s use of priming as a metric found that while students demonstrated high linguistic competency, their level of syntactic priming was low. This finding proves that theoretical knowledge does not directly correlate with the ability to use complex syntactic structures. This gap provides a key rationale for SynTutor, which aims to combine theoretical linguistic knowledge with a visual syntax tree to transform passive knowledge into active structural learning.  
	The question of AI's effectiveness in increasing learner understanding and competence is also explored by local literature. Dela Cruz (2025) investigated the integration of AI into English Classroom Practices in the Philippine higher education system. Analyzing how emerging technologies can address traditional language challenges, the study utilized qualitative and quantitative data from 43 teachers, 158 students, and 3 administrators. The research concluded that AI is effectively used to promote an adaptive and data-informed language education experience. This successful integration is a core tenet of SynTutor, which aims to utilize the same technology to provide interpretable feedback and guide learners toward a deeper understanding of linguistics. Further research also demonstrates that utilizing AI correlates with positive improvements in student performance for English language courses. A descriptive research design identified positive correlations in language improvement, confidence enhancement, and attitude, covering the four core skills of writing, reading, listening, and speaking. Based on these results, researchers have advocated for the use of AI in structurally shaping positive attitudes in learning the English language, which provides evidence for how SynTutor aims to improve a learner’s comprehension compared to traditional software and linguistic learning tools.  
A study by Magday et al. (2024) tested the effectiveness of an application integrated with artificial intelligence named “CiCi” to enhance the subject-verb agreement (SVA) skills of learners from the Philippines. Used as a supplemental learning tool, wherein a group consisting of 20 Grade 7 students underwent an intervention program, while another 20 students underwent traditional method of learning of SVA. The results of the study showed that the experimental group that used CiCi significantly improved their skills. Those who were taught through the traditional method did not show any significant improvement in comparison. The study portrays how the use of an AI-integrated tutor contributes in creating innovative teaching strategies, applicable in the field of linguistics and improving a learner’s English ability. The themes that the study found: free charges, user-friendly features, fun english learning experiences, and providing fun exercises align with how a similar application like SynTutor can be used for increasing a learner’s competence, while utilizing technology.  
	Reinforcing the importance of transforming theoretical knowledge into practical application, Cartilero (2024) similarly evaluates the relationship between syntactic priming, speech acts, and linguistic competence among Senior High School students. This research identified a “low” level of syntactic priming despite “high” linguistic competence, suggesting that students often struggle with the cognitive process of reusing specific sentence structures even if they know the grammatical rules. SynTutor directly addresses this gap. By providing real-time visualization of phrase structures, the system serves as a cognitive scaffold that reinforces syntactic priming, allowing students to move beyond the passive rule-memorization noted by Cartilero and towards an active exploration of how sentence structures are built and reused.  
Furthermore, the importance of building robust computational linguistic resources is highlighted by Arañes (2022), who explored the scarcity of parsed and labeled corpora for the Cebuano language. To address this, the research developed the “GJA Cebuano Treebank” to adapt Universal Dependencies (UD) treebanks for Cebuano, enabling automated text processing and syntactic analysis. SynTutor builds upon this critical development in automated syntax generators by incorporating guidelines for resolving the structural ambiguities that often hinder parsing algorithms. This foundational research thus provides a key framework for a tutoring system designed to explain the hierarchical relationships of sentence structures to learners.  
The need for educational focus over mere correction is reinforced by the systematic literature review of Cano et al. (2024), which evaluated various NLP grammar correction programs. The authors reviewed 40 studies, identifying common algorithms, deep learning methodologies (including Word2Vec, LSTM-CRF, and neural networks), and datasets utilized. While the review proposed improvements to grammar-checking tools, suggesting they incorporate learning support to reduce recurring errors, the authors noted a persistent limitation: existing systems remain largely focused on correction and suggested outputs rather than delivering clear, user-facing explanations that support deeper learning. This finding is highly pertinent to SynTutor, as it outlines the current state of NLP-based grammar checking in Philippine schooling while highlighting the continuing lack of explainable and educational feedback in contemporary applications.  
Further supporting the case for advanced AI integration, Soriano et al. (2024) researched the impact of using Meta’s AI writing tool(s) on the academic writing skills of 60 Filipino university students in ESL classes. Utilizing a pre-test/post-test design, the data showed statistically significant increases in performance across all measured outcomes (e.g., grammar, coherence, and overall structure), with calculated effect sizes (Cohen’s d) representing large improvements for each area. The results, grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Constructivist Learning Theory, indicate that AI-assisted writing tools boost motivation, engagement, and overall writing performance. However, the study did not examine how these systems provide structured grammatical explanations that promote deeper understanding rather than just performance improvement. This provides local justification for developing SynTutor as a feedback-driven and explanation-based grammar learning tool for Filipino learners.  
Finally, Domingo (2025) investigated the relationship between AI-driven writing tools and Impostor Syndrome among 200 tertiary ESL students at a Philippine state university. Using a mixed-methods explanatory sequential design, the study found that frequent reliance on automated drafting tools resulted in 24.5% of respondents experiencing impostor biases, though only 2.5% indicated intense feelings of impostor syndrome. While AI improved writing self-efficacy and decreased anxiety due to real-time feedback, Domingo warned that excessive reliance could inhibit the development of mature, independent writing skills, raising concerns about authenticity and academic integrity. These findings underscore a critical point: current AI tools, due to their correction-based designs and lack of transparent, explanation-driven feedback, often encourage passive reliance. This powerfully reinforces the necessity for systems like SynTutor that are designed to promote active learning by helping users understand grammatical principles rather than simply providing corrections.
